word_order: other, with a one-line justification from the sample: main clauses show verb-second order while embedded/relative clauses are verb-final (e.g. 'dunkle energie ist ...' vs 'die permanent auf das universum einwirkt').
register: formal written informational/encyclopedic (concise, factual sentences like encyclopedia or newswire prose).
fillers_and_hesitations: none observed (no explicit hesitation particles in the sample)
discourse_markers: subordinating conjunctions that introduce embedded clauses (als, damit, wenn, dass)
coordinating conjunctions that link clauses or list items (und)
relative-clause introducers / relative pronouns that connect modifiers to nouns (die, der, das)
clause_boundary_signals: verb-position alternation (finite verb appears early in main clauses (V2) but at the end of embedded/relative clauses (V-final))
subordinating conjunctions / complementizers and relative pronouns that introduce embedded clauses
coordinating conjunctions that join full clauses
non_boundary_traps: article/relative-pronoun homonyms (die/der/das) which look like clause starters but may be simple determiners
nominal enumerations / coordinated noun lists (series of nouns or verbal-nominal gerunds) that resemble multiple clauses but form one nominal constituent
prepositional noun phrases following nouns (in X, im Y) that can look like clause breaks but are modifiers
unstable_prefix_signals: article/relative-pronoun homonyms (das/die/der) — early token can be either determiner or clause introducer, later context decides
als (comparative vs subordinator) — immediate interpretation can flip once the following phrase appears
coordinating conjunctions (und) — may indicate a short list or the continuation of a longer coordinated phrase, so earlier unit boundaries remain provisional
notes_for_prompt_writer: Main clauses typically show verb-second (finite verb early) while embedded and relative clauses are verb-final; many clauses are introduced by subordinating conjunctions or relative pronouns. Definite articles and relative pronouns are formally identical and frequently cause local ambiguity. German sentences in the sample are noun-phrase heavy and use nominal coordination (lists) without verbs, so sequences of nouns and determiners often belong to a single constituent rather than separate clauses.
